sources: A Quick Guide to the Government's Healthy Eating Recommendations (Public Health England, 2018)
Government Dietary Recommendations: energy and nutrients for males/females aged 1-18 and 19+ (Public Health England, 2016)

eatwell_guide_principles.guidance: Over a third of the diet should come from fruit and vegetables. Eat at least 5 portions of a variety of fruit and veg every day. A portion is about 80g.
eatwell_guide_principles.lunchbox_application: Aim to include at least 1-2 portions in a packed lunch (e.g. cherry tomatoes, carrot sticks, a piece of fruit), counted across the whole day's meals.
eatwell_guide_principles.caveats: Limit 100% fruit/vegetable juice and smoothies to a combined 150ml/day, consumed with meals (not as a between-meal snack) to reduce tooth decay risk. Dried fruit (30g) counts as one portion but should be eaten at mealtimes, not as a snack, for the same reason.

eatwell_guide_principles.food_group: Potatoes, bread, rice, pasta and other starchy carbohydrates
eatwell_guide_principles.guidance: Base meals on starchy carbohydrates, choosing wholegrain versions where possible (wholemeal bread, wholewheat pasta, brown rice).
eatwell_guide_principles.lunchbox_application: The bread/wrap/pitta/bagel base of a lunchbox sandwich should ideally be wholegrain; mixing one white and one wholegrain slice is a reasonable compromise for children who dislike wholegrain.

eatwell_guide_principles.guidance: Include some dairy and alternatives, choosing lower-fat and lower-sugar options (e.g. semi-skimmed or skimmed milk, lower-fat/lower-sugar yoghurt, lower-fat cheese).
eatwell_guide_principles.lunchbox_application: A small yoghurt or a portion of milk in a lunchbox is a good way to meet this; choose reduced-fat cheese where used as a filling.

eatwell_guide_principles.food_group: Beans, pulses, fish, eggs, meat and other proteins
eatwell_guide_principles.guidance: Eat some protein-rich foods including 2 portions of fish per week, one of which is oily (salmon, sardines, mackerel, kippers). No more than 70g red/processed meat per day on average.
eatwell_guide_principles.lunchbox_application: Rotate fish-based lunches (tuna, salmon) and pulse-based lunches (hummus, beans) alongside meat-based ones across the school week to build variety and meet the fish quota.

eatwell_guide_principles.guidance: Choose unsaturated oils and spreads and use in small amounts.
eatwell_guide_principles.lunchbox_application: Use lower-fat spreads sparingly on sandwiches.

eatwell_guide_principles.food_group: Foods high in fat, salt and sugar
eatwell_guide_principles.guidance: Foods such as chocolate, cakes, biscuits, full-sugar soft drinks, crisps should be eaten less often and in small amounts; they are not necessary in the diet.
eatwell_guide_principles.lunchbox_application: Limit crisps and sweet treats to occasional inclusion; swap for homemade plain popcorn, plain rice cakes, fruit teacakes, or fruit (fresh/dried/tinned in juice).

eatwell_guide_principles.guidance: Aim for 6-8 glasses of fluid a day; water, lower-fat milk, and sugar-free drinks (including tea/coffee for adults) all count.
eatwell_guide_principles.lunchbox_application: Water or milk is the best lunchbox drink choice; if including fruit juice, limit to 150ml combined with any other juice/smoothie consumed that day.

energy_distribution_convention.note: By convention, based on an average 2000kcal/day woman's energy requirement (figures will scale differently for children, see age-band tables below):

child_age_band_recommendations.note: Values drawn from Government Dietary Recommendations (PHE 2016) Tables 1, 3 and 5. Energy figures for 11-18 are capped at 2500kcal/day (males) and 2000kcal/day (females) for obesity prevention. A rough rule-of-thumb lunch target is about 25-30% of daily energy, consistent with the ~600kcal lunch convention.

age_11_14.note_iron: Higher iron recommendation for females 11-18 reflects menstrual losses; SACN notes this may still be insufficient for those with heavy menstrual losses, where supplementation may be the practical solution.

school_safe_constraints: Many UK primary schools operate a 'nut-free' policy across the whole school (not just for individual allergic children) due to the severity and prevalence of nut allergies; lunches should avoid peanuts and tree nuts entirely when a school is flagged as nut-free.

Schools, as institutional caterers, are legally required to identify children's allergies and ensure safe food is provided (see allergen_rules knowledge base); a lunch recommendation system must treat any stated allergy as an absolute exclusion, not a soft preference.

Fizzy/sugary drinks and confectionery are commonly restricted or discouraged in UK school lunchbox policies, consistent with the 'eat less often, in small amounts' guidance for high fat/salt/sugar foods.
Dried fruit and fruit juice, while counting toward 5-a-day, are best limited to mealtimes only (not snack-time) due to tooth decay risk, which is relevant when scheduling a lunch versus a snack.
